title: Nvidia's board under fire for handling of CEO's alleged affairs
description:
Even as Jensen Huang has returned to work, Nvidia's board is facing criticism over how it handled the crisis brought on by the CEO's alleged affairs.

MICHEL MARTIN, HOST: How did a board that unanimously decided that its CEO must go decide a few days later to bring him right back? We're talking about Nvidia and its founder, former and now current CEO Jensen Huang. NPR's Andrea Hsu has been gathering reaction to the board's handling of the crisis, and she's with us now to tell us more.Good morning, Andrea.ANDREA HSU, BYLINE: Good morning.MARTIN: OK, so let me just point out here that at an all-hands meeting on Tuesday, Huang apologized for hurting his family and violating the company's code of conduct. That's according to a livestream of the meeting which was viewed by The New York Times. He also reportedly said that President Trump didn't pressure the board into bringing him back. NPR has reached out to Nvidia for confirmation of this, but hasn't heard back. You've been hearing from people who know how boards are meant to operate. What are you hearing from them?HSU: Yeah. Well, there's been criticism from both those who think Jensen Huang shouldn't have been brought back and also those who think it was the right thing to do. And, Michel, let's remember the role of boards - they exist to make informed and deliberate decisions that are in the best interests of the company and its shareholders. In many instances, they are the only mechanism of accountability for companies and CEOs. And in the case of Nvidia, you know, a lot of people say the board fell short on these duties, and we've asked Nvidia for a response to that, but we haven't heard back on that, either.MARTIN: Now, recognizing that you're getting a range of opinions there, do these experts have thoughts on what should have happened?HSU: Yeah. Well, many are saying that the board should have made different choices. Our colleague Shannon Bond spoke with Rob Lalka. He's a professor at Tulane's Freeman School of Business (ph), and he points out that in the last decade, there have been a number of high-profile cases similar to what allegedly happened at Nvidia - you know, a CEO having an affair with an employee. It happened at Intel, McDonald's, Nestle. And Lalka says those boards followed their policies, and those CEOs were out. They decided it had to happen to preserve company values and credibility. But then, as for Nvidia, here's what Lalka says.ROB LALKA: The board basically went around its entire process that it had set in place for that investigation to put him back into power.MARTIN: But you also mentioned that there are people who think bringing Huang back was the right thing to do. Say more about that.HSU: Yeah. I spoke with Betsy Atkins. She is a three-time CEO, a tech entrepreneur and someone who served on several dozen boards. And she is in the camp of people who say, look, Jensen Huang is not just any CEO. He is a genius founder, someone who built this multi-trillion dollar company from nothing.BETSY ATKINS: I'm not saying that you get to break the law and break all the rules, but it requires nuanced business judgment to weigh many other factors.HSU: And her complaint is that Nvidia's board acted too quickly in forcing Huang out. She says the real litmus test for board members is do they have courage and conviction and character to do the right thing and to withstand pressure when times are difficult? And she thinks Nvidia's board failed this test, essentially. But now that Huang is back, her hope is that the board can go back to focusing on what she calls the business of the business.MARTIN: OK. But given that Nvidia, as she pointed out, is such a powerful, high-profile company, such a big footprint in the economy, what signal is this board's flip-flop sending more broadly?HSU: Yeah. Well, people I've talked to this week says it just drives home the idea that in Silicon Valley, all that matters really is money. Rob Lalka, the business professor, takes it a step further. He describes the board's decision to bring Jensen Huang back as rash and aimed at boosting short-term profits. He says that doesn't make for a robust economy. And he points out that AI leaders have repeatedly said they want to do what's in the best long-term interests of humanity. And he says what's unfolded at Nvidia speaks to quite the opposite.MARTIN: That is NPR's Andrea Hsu.Andrea, thank you.HSU: Thank you, Michel.(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC) Copyright © 2026 NPR.
